title: Apple Completes the Set: Every Magnificent Seven Stock Opts Out of OKX-ICE Venue
detail:
Apple Completes the Set: Every Magnificent Seven Stock Opts Out of OKX-ICE Venue
Decrypt Staff
Sat, November 7, 2026 at 11:01 AM CST 2 min read
META
AAPL
MSFT
GOOG
AMZN
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Every member of Wall Street's "Magnificent Seven" now wants its stock kept off OKX and ICE's planned tokenized stock venue.

Apple and Meta Platforms are among 11 companies added to the list of objecting issuers in an updated notice from OKXICE TSV dated Thursday.

They join Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia and Tesla, completing a sweep by the group of tech giants that makes up a large share of the S&P 500's value. The other new objectors are Home Depot, Boeing, GE Vernova, Palantir, ServiceNow, S&P Global, KLA, Super Micro Computer and Nebius Group, bringing the total number of companies saying "no" to the OKX and ICE platform to 67.

Meta's objection carries some irony. The Facebook parent once tried to launch its own stablecoin, Libra, later renamed Diem, before abandoning the project in 2022 amid regulatory pushback.

Apple had been one of the last megacaps missing from the list after Amazon, Tesla, and SpaceX objected in the venue's Nov. 2 notice. The tally stood at 56 then, and at nine on Oct. 15, when the first objectors appeared.

Just as notable is who hasn't objected. Crypto-friendly public companies such as Coinbase, Robinhood and Strategy don't appear on the list. Coinbase launched tokenized stocks for non-U.S. users on its Base network in August. Berkshire Hathaway, Visa, and Exxon Mobil are also absent. It's unclear whether OKXICE notified those companies.

Under the SEC's innovation exemption, which the agency unveiled in September after the Clarity Act failed to advance in the Senate, a venue must notify a company before offering a version of its shares tokenized by an unaffiliated third party. If the company objects in writing within 30 days, the venue can't make that stock available for trading, according to the SEC's order. It's worth noting, though, that the objection applies only to that venue.

OKXICE TSV, a 50-50 joint venture between NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange and OKX's U.S. holding company, plans to offer tokenized U.S. stocks 24/7 through permissioned pools on OKX's XLayer blockchain. An outside "tokenizer" would hold real shares one-for-one through a registered broker-dealer.

With the market's biggest names opted out, it's unclear which major stocks the venue will be able to offer at launch, and its notices don't list the tokens it plans to make available.

title: Snap Will Stop Reporting Daily Users in 2027. Its 92 Million North Americans Explain Why
detail:
Snap Will Stop Reporting Daily Users in 2027. Its 92 Million North Americans Explain Why
Rexielyn Diaz

SNAP
META
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Snap Will Stop Reporting Daily Users in 2027. Its 92 Million North Americans Explain Why ©Tero Vesalainen from Getty Images and mohamed abdelghaffar from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

Snap will switch its main audience metric from daily to monthly users in 2027, after third-quarter daily users of 495 million missed estimates.

Revenue rose 14% to $1.72 billion, slightly light, but Snap swung to a $56 million profit from a $104 million loss.

Snap's advertising grew 4%, while Meta's advertising revenue jumped 26% to $63.1 billion in the same quarter.

Snap's early February report must show ad growth picking up alongside fourth-quarter adjusted EBITDA guided to $490 million to $525 million.

Snap (SNAP:NYSE) is changing how it keeps score. Starting with the first quarter of 2027, monthly active users replace daily users as its headline audience number.

The switch arrived next to a miss. Third-quarter daily users came in at 495 million against the 499 million analysts expected, and North American daily users fell 6% to 92 million.

Advertising is the wider gap. Snap's ad revenue grew 4% last quarter, while Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) grew advertising 26% to $63.1 billion over the same three months.

Shares closed Friday at $4.96, down 39% this year.

Fewer daily users, more profit

Here's the quarter Snap reported on Nov. 4:

Revenue rose 14% to $1.72 billion, a touch below the roughly $1.73 billion consensus.

Net income came in at $56 million, or $0.03 a share, against a $104 million loss a year earlier.

Adjusted EBITDA climbed to $383 million from $182 million.

Management tied the new metric to a push for more profitable growth, with less money spent buying daily users.

North America shows why that matters. It holds 19% of Snap's daily users yet produces 59% of revenue, and its daily count peaked at 101 million in 2023.

Monthly users rose 4% to 977 million, so the new headline number starts within sight of a billion. And sales kept rising through the user slump…

Snap (SNAP): total revenue, quarterly, $ billions, Q3 2024–Q3 2026 (TIKR)

Growth did slow, though, to 14% from 19% in the second quarter.

Subscriptions are paying the bills

Other revenue, mostly subscriptions, jumped 84% to $350 million, and paid subscribers passed 30 million.

CEO Evan Spiegel said in the results release that "AI is becoming a significant advantage for our teams and advertising platform." Meta can point to proof: its ad prices rose 14% and impressions 10%. Snap's ad line grew 4%.

Costs are the cleaner win. Total costs and expenses rose under 1% to $1.65 billion while revenue added $216 million. Where does that leave margins?

Snap (SNAP): gross margin (%), quarterly, Q3 2024–Q3 2026 (TIKR)

Subscription dollars carry richer margins, which helps explain how EBITDA doubled on 14% growth.

Snap guided fourth-quarter revenue to $1.95 billion to $1.985 billion and adjusted EBITDA to $490 million to $525 million. The revenue midpoint sits slightly above the $1.948 billion consensus.

Dan Ives: Big Tech Free Cash Flow "Will Trough in 1H2027" as Capex Growth Peaks Early ©da-kuk from Getty Images Signature and CG6 Images from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co. now expects Big Tech's capex growth to peak in 2027, and free cash flow at Microsoft, Meta, Alphabet and Amazon to bottom in the first half of that year.

Analysts' consensus for Microsoft already shows the trough and rebound Ives describes.

Amazon and Meta are deeper in the hole: Meta's third-quarter capex outran its operating cash, and Amazon's free cash flow, on TIKR's measure, fell to $7.7 billion in 2025.

Ives has the bottom about right, but the full payoff still looks like a 2029 story.

Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co. now thinks the cash squeeze at Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ), Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ), Alphabet (GOOG) and Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ) will end sooner than he expected.

In a post on X on Nov. 5, he wrote that "Big Tech capex growth rate now peaks in 2027 vs our previous view that would not happen until 2028/2029." He pointed to the midterm results, especially in Texas, where he expects the data center buildout to slow.

In a follow-up, he tied it to cash: "Free cash flow will trough in 1H2027 and starting in the 2H of next year will start to show a trajectory towards a major rebound in 2028 and massive FCF ramp in 2029-2030."

Bloomberg Intelligence's Mandeep Singh put a number on it. On the Bloomberg Intelligence podcast on Nov. 4, he pointed to Texas data centers and said: "2027 capex could be revised lower by 5 to 7%."

Microsoft's Numbers Already Look Like This

Microsoft's fiscal year ends in June, so its fiscal 2027 includes the first half of 2027, where Ives puts the trough. Analysts expect free cash flow to fall to $34.0 billion that year, about half of fiscal 2026's $67.0 billion, then rebound to $52.3 billion in fiscal 2028.

MSFT Free Cash Flow, Actual and Consensus Estimates: Fiscal 2024-2028 (TIKR)

Microsoft's free cash flow already fell to $18.6 billion in its September quarter from $25.7 billion a year earlier, and a day after that report it sold $25 billion of bonds, its first US investment-grade sale since 2017.

Microsoft was the only one of the five biggest hyperscalers, counting Oracle, whose free cash flow stayed positive in the third quarter.

Amazon and Meta Have the Deeper Hole

On TIKR's measure, Amazon's free cash flow fell to $7.7 billion in 2025, from $32.9 billion in 2024.

AMZN Free Cash Flow: 2021-2025 (TIKR)

Meta's purchases of property and equipment nearly doubled to $69.7 billion in 2025, from $37.3 billion.

META Capital Expenditures: 2021-2025 (TIKR)

Meta's third-quarter capex, including finance-lease principal payments, rose 80% to $34.9 billion, more than the $32.8 billion its operations brought in, and on Oct. 26 it said it plans to sell up to $95 billion of stock. Alphabet burned $9.07 billion of cash in the quarter, according to Reuters.

title: Mark Zuckerberg’s fortune tops $200 billion. His 3 daughters won’t inherit most of it
detail:
Mark Zuckerberg’s fortune tops $200 billion. His 3 daughters won’t inherit most of it
Mark Zuckerberg, chief executive officer of Meta Platforms Inc., speaks during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, California, on Wednesday, Sept. 23, 2026. · Fortune · Minh Connors/Bloomberg via Getty Images
Emma Witman
Sat, November 7, 2026 at 3:30 AM CST 3 min read
META
Trade META on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

When Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan pledged to give away 99% of their Facebook shares in 2015, the stake was worth about $45 billion. Zuckerberg's fortune now exceeds $200 billion, and their three daughters still aren't slated to inherit most of it.

That puts the Meta CEO and Chan, a pediatrician, in a cohort of ultra-wealthy households, including Bill Gates, Warren Buffett, and Michael Bloomberg, where the children won't be inheriting the bulk of the balance sheet.

The couple announced the decision in December 2015, after the birth of their first child, Maxima. In an open letter to their newborn, they introduced the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative (CZI) and committed to giving away 99% of their Facebook (now Meta) shares during their lifetimes.

"Like all parents, we want you to grow up in a world better than ours today," they wrote. "Our society has an obligation to invest now to improve the lives of all those coming into this world, not just those already here."

The pledge stands out against a larger backdrop: an estimated $124 trillion is expected to pass to younger generations as baby boomers hand down their portfolios.

California's billionaire tax looks set to miss his fortune

Zuckerberg's fortune also looks unlikely to be hit by California's proposed "billionaire tax." Proposition 40, a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of the state's billionaires, was trailing 55% to 45% as of Nov. 6, with ballots still being counted.

Proposition 42, a billionaire-backed countermeasure that would nullify the tax and bar new wealth taxes in California, was leading with about 54% support.

Zuckerberg had told Meta's board he was weighing a move out of the state over the measure. The company responded by creating a new class of stock he could sell to cover a potential bill.

Why CZI is an LLC, not a foundation

The structure of the couple's philanthropy is notable. CZI is a limited liability company rather than a conventional private foundation, which gives the couple flexibility over timing and cause areas and lets them invest in for-profit companies and fund policy advocacy.

Gates took the foundation route. The Gates Foundation now plans to close in 2045 after spending down roughly $200 billion.

Gates, for his part, cited Zuckerberg as a model of giving in a conversation with Fortune last year. "There are exemplars like Mark Zuckerberg, you know, through the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, is committed to give over 90% of his wealth away and he's off to a very good start," Gates said.

"He's someone I talked to about a lot of things, including philanthropy, and they do education research; we partner on some of that."

Big Tech's $1 Trillion Rally Bets Regulation Won't Touch "the Profits of the Tech Companies" ©Worawee Meepian's Images and Yakobchuk from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Apple, Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft and Meta were on pace to add nearly $1 trillion on Wednesday after Democrats won Congress. On Thursday, the four hyperscalers gave back 2% to 4%.

New York Assemblymember Alex Bores says investors bet on tight limits on new data centers and no rules that hit Big Tech's profits.

Trump's veto threat makes new federal AI laws unlikely before 2029. California's governor-elect is a separate risk.

Microsoft trades near its one-year average forward P/E, leaving little room for rules that cut expected profits.

On Nov. 4, investors cheered the Democratic sweep by piling into Big Tech. Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ), Alphabet (GOOG), Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ) and Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ), along with Apple, were on pace to add nearly $1 trillion in market value, by Bloomberg's count, and Microsoft closed at a record.

Democrats ran on slowing the AI build-out. Investors read that as a brake on the spending that has pushed free cash flow negative at Amazon, Alphabet and Meta. Neoclouds like CoreWeave sank.

On the Nov. 5 episode of Prof G Markets, Alex Bores, a New York Assembly member and author of the RAISE Act, said the move "expresses a bet that there will be stringent regulation on building new data centers, that that capacity will be curtailed, but that there won't be regulations that impact the profits of the tech companies and the AI companies."

He doesn't buy the second half, saying it doesn't match what he hears from voters or elected officials.

By Thursday, the mood had turned. The Nasdaq 100 fell about 6% in a broad chip and AI selloff, and the four hyperscalers gave back 2% to 4% each.

Big Tech Has a Lot of Profit to Protect

The money at stake is the earnings growth Wall Street already expects. Consensus has Alphabet's normalized EPS rising from $10.81 in 2025 to $18.23 in 2028:

GOOG Normalized EPS, Actual and Consensus Estimates: 2023-2028 (TIKR)

That's 69% more in three years.

Investors aren't paying much of a premium for that growth. Microsoft trades at 26x forward earnings, a touch above its one-year average of 25x and well below the 31x it hit last November:

MSFT Stock NTM P/E: 1-Year (TIKR)

At that multiple, the price assumes the profit path holds, with little room for a rule that cuts into it.

Over the past year, Booking Holdings (BKNG) stock lost 17.5%, dividends included, compared with a 9.8% return for the S&P 500. This performance marked the worst return within a peer group of five that includes Meta Platforms, Airbnb, Expedia and Hyatt Hotels. The lag occurred even though Meta is the only company in the group that converts a larger share of sales into operating profit than Booking does. So what do Booking's rivals offer that Booking does not?

Booking Is More Profitable Than Airbnb But Grows Slower

Most competitors offer faster sales growth. Airbnb operates in the same hotel and resort industry and provides the starkest contrast. During the four fiscal quarters ended September 30, 2026, Booking retained 32.8% of its revenue as operating profit, compared with 22.5% at Airbnb. Yet Booking reported revenue growth of 8.0% over those quarters, which is about half of Airbnb's 16.7% pace. That figure is held down by a $900 million legal charge, linked to an FTC action, that cut third-quarter revenue.

Investors pay far less for that profit, pricing the stock at 16.8 times earnings compared with 34.9 for Airbnb. Meta Platforms generates nearly the exact same margin as Booking, but its revenue expanded 27.5%. Meta is the only other comparable company priced above Booking on an earnings basis. Part of our series on building a mix that lasts. Start here: is 60/40 dead?

Which is real? Both, and the gap between them is the interesting part. In dollars, your S&P 500 fund rose about three-quarters in three years. Measured against gold, it lost ground, because gold did even better. We'll go stock by stock through the biggest names to see who really beat it. Here's what the pros are actually working on, though: not which ruler is right, but what share of their money would hold its value if the dollar keeps losing ground to hard assets. We'll come back to that, with a rule you can set this weekend.

What Does Everyone Already Know?

That stocks have had a great run. Our price data shows the S&P 500 fund SPY up 75.0% over three years, with dividends, from the close on November 6, 2023, to Friday's close.

What fewer people notice is that gold did better. Over the same three years, the gold fund GLD rose about 103%. Divide one by the other and the S&P 500, priced in ounces of gold, fell about 14%.

So Which Number Is Real?

Your bills are in dollars, so the dollar number is the one you live on. If your $100,000 became about $175,000, you can spend $175,000. That's real.

The gold number answers a different question: how much of that gain came from the companies, and how much from the dollar itself buying less? Gold doesn't earn anything, and nobody can print more of it. When stocks beat gold, the businesses outran the currency. When gold beats stocks, part of what looked like growth was the measuring stick shrinking. Over the last three years, by this measure, the stick shrank faster than the average business grew.

A simple way to see it on your own statement: take your balance three years ago and today, and divide each by the gold price on those dates. If the number of ounces went down, your money grew in dollars but lost ground against a hard asset. That doesn't mean you lost money; your groceries are still priced in dollars. It means your plan has been quietly riding on the dollar.

The question worth a quiet weekend isn't what Monday does. It's where your money needs to be in 2031, and whether Thursday changes that. We'll get there with data: what the market did five years after its worst days, and what the biggest companies looked like five years after past selloffs.

What Does Everyone Already Know?

On Thursday, using the big index funds as stand-ins, the S&P 500 (SPY) fell 4.4% to $733.00 and the Nasdaq-100 (QQQ) 6.5%. Nvidia fell 9.3% to $181.60. Gold and long Treasuries edged up. Both funds rose on Friday, but SPY ended the week down 2.7% and QQQ down 5.0%.

It was the AI trade unwinding: the chip makers and the companies building the power and data centers behind AI fell hardest. Power is the bottleneck, opposition to new data centers is growing town by town, and the new Congress can lean on both; on Wednesday, Meta's president told a Wall Street Journal conference that the midterm results will make building data centers harder. We flagged power as the AI trade's real risk on Nov 2, in "Nvidia Stock's Real Risk Isn't China. It's Power."

The weekend question is the natural one: what happens Monday? We already looked at the short run, and after the 21 earlier days like Thursday the next week was close to a coin flip. So let's use the quiet of a Saturday to look the other way, five years out, to November 2031.

"The question in front of you is rarely the one that will matter in five years." - Anonymous

Between the end of 2002 and Thursday, the S&P 500 fell at least 3.5% on the same day the Nasdaq Composite fell at least 5% just 21 times. Eighteen of them are more than five years old. Here's where the S&P 500 stood five years after each, grouped by episode, price only:
